summaries.headline: NYC's New Teachers Confront AI, Class Size Mandates
summaries.summary: More than 4,000 new teachers gathered at Barclays Center for NYC orientation as the district works toward hiring roughly 6,600 teachers this year to meet a state mandate capping class sizes at 20-25 students. New hires voiced concern about students outsourcing thinking to AI even as they await the city's delayed AI policy guidance, while Chancellor Kamar Samuels warned incoming teachers to brace for a difficult first year, invoking his own rocky start in the classroom. The hiring push comes as New York teachers report lower morale than the national average, a gap that could shape how many of these new recruits stick around long enough to become veterans.

summaries.headline: Philadelphia's $25M Reading Curriculum Hits Turbulence
summaries.summary: Philadelphia is entering year three of a $25 million overhaul of its K-8 English language arts curriculum, and a new district research report reveals significant implementation problems from year one. Focus groups with more than 100 teachers, principals, and administrators surfaced complaints about weak phonics instruction, insufficient time for students to read full books, and little support for struggling or behind-grade-level readers, while most principals still called the EL Education curriculum "a step in the right direction." State test results back up the concern: reading proficiency actually dropped after the curriculum's first year, with only about one-third of K-8 students proficient, far short of the district's goal of surpassing 50% by 2030, and this fall's new scores will show whether recent fixes like added flex days and K-2 literacy support are moving the needle.

summaries.headline: Gates Warns AI Could Shrink Student Learning
summaries.summary: Bill Gates is sounding an alarm on artificial intelligence's classroom impact, warning in a nearly 6,000-word essay that the same tool promising to expand learning could just as easily undermine it. The Microsoft co-founder points to a 2025 study suggesting heavy reliance on AI tools correlates with weaker critical thinking and retention among users. Coming from one of tech's most prominent boosters of education innovation, the caution signals that even AI's champions see real risk in how quickly schools are adopting the technology without guardrails.

summaries.headline: Reframing the Screen Time vs. EdTech Debate
summaries.summary: District leaders face growing pressure to restrict student screen time even as schools remain deeply invested in one-to-one devices and digital curriculum. The tension isn't really about screens versus no screens, but about distinguishing passive consumption from purposeful, instructionally-driven technology use — a distinction that gets lost in blanket policy debates. Leaders who can articulate that difference to parents and staff are better positioned to defend edtech investments while still taking wellness concerns seriously.

summaries.headline: Chicago Board Candidates Pledge to Ban AI
summaries.summary: Roughly half of the 45 candidates running for Chicago's first fully elected school board have signed a pledge to ban AI use by students and educators for three years, alongside eliminating screen time before third grade and hiring a chief privacy officer. The pledge, crafted by Illinois Families for Public Schools, also demands a ban on collecting student biometric data like voice recordings from literacy software, part of a broader national parent backlash against ed-tech tools. Critics, including former CPS CEO Janice Jackson, argue an outright ban abdicates the district's responsibility to teach students to navigate AI safely rather than avoid it altogether, setting up a policy fight that will likely shape how the new board approaches technology governance from day one.

summaries.headline: Colorado's Low-Performance Watchlist Shrinks
summaries.summary: Colorado's preliminary 2026 school performance ratings show more than 50 schools exiting the state's accountability clock, including Abraham Lincoln High in Denver and the Aurora Central Campus. Nearly two-thirds of the state's 1,700-plus schools earned the top green rating, a slight dip from last year, while 55% of districts and co-ops earned high ratings, matching 2025 figures. Both Denver Public Schools and Jeffco Public Schools, the state's two largest districts, held onto green ratings for a second consecutive year, signaling stability at the top even as the overall accountability picture continues to improve.

summaries.headline: NYC Bans Student AI Tools Through Middle School
summaries.summary: New York City's Education Department is set to release AI guidance banning generative AI tools, including chatbots and AI tutors, for students from 2-K through eighth grade, while also restricting individual devices for the youngest learners and capping screen time at 30 minutes for grades 3-5 and 45 minutes for middle schoolers. High schoolers will get restricted AI access tied to literacy and career readiness goals, with five pilot programs testing broader use, and teachers can use approved AI for lesson planning and translation but not grading, behavior monitoring, or special education plans. As the nation's largest school system takes this notably cautious stance, districts nationwide will be watching closely to see whether restriction—rather than integration—becomes the dominant model for K-12 AI policy.

summaries.headline: NYC Bans Student AI Tools in K-8
summaries.summary: New York City will prohibit student-facing generative AI tools like chatbots in pre-K through eighth grade classrooms while permitting limited use in high schools, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced just eight days before the school year starts. The city says it's disabling AI features on 38 software programs already used in schools but hasn't disclosed which products are affected, and officials have acknowledged they lack solid data on current AI use across the district's 1,600 schools, having declined to release survey results on the topic. The policy—billed as the nation's broadest generative AI moratorium—leaves unresolved questions about how officials will judge acceptable AI levels in tech products and enforce the rules, drawing both cautious praise from moratorium advocates and warnings from education leaders that the abrupt rollout will disrupt tools teachers already rely on.

summaries.headline: Newark Teen's Education Derailed by Self-Deportation
summaries.summary: A 16-year-old Newark student named Bruno is leaving behind his junior-year college coursework, friends, and church community as his family self-deports to Brazil, choosing to leave on their own terms rather than risk ICE detention. His parents, who arrived in the U.S. in 2022 seeking better opportunities for their children, join more than a million immigrants who have opted for voluntary departure since President Trump took office, according to Department of Homeland Security data. For Bruno, whose K-12 education was already disrupted by the pandemic and the challenges of learning English in a new country, the move threatens to nullify his high school and college credits and upend a carefully built academic timeline, leaving districts and educators to reckon with how immigration enforcement policy is reshaping students' educational trajectories mid-course.

summaries.headline: Chronic Absenteeism Keeps Climbing in North Carolina
summaries.summary: Nearly one in four North Carolina students were chronically absent during the 2024-25 school year, missing more than 10% of classes, and the rate climbs to one in three among students experiencing poverty — 10 percentage points above pre-pandemic levels. Research shows the threshold for concern is lower than most assume: 18 or more missed days a year can derail early reading and math skills, and absenteeism as early as sixth grade raises the odds a student eventually drops out, with even a few absences in the month before state testing measurably denting math scores. The effects don't stay contained to individual students, either, since classrooms with high absenteeism rates drag down achievement for regularly attending peers as teachers divert time to help students catch up.

summaries.headline: Edtech Failures Trace to Implementation, Not Screens
summaries.summary: A former superintendent argues that the wave of legislative screen-time crackdowns—Los Angeles Unified's unanimous vote to ban district-issued devices in early grades, cap screen time, and audit all edtech contracts, plus active legislation in at least 17 states and signed laws in four—misdiagnoses the real problem in classroom technology. Drawing on firsthand experience, the author contrasts districts that handed teachers device carts with no instructional plan or support against a school that invested heavily in professional development and let teachers decide when and how to use a defined set of tools, with outcomes to show for it. The piece suggests blanket bans risk treating a symptom of poor implementation as if it were the disease, leaving the harder work of building teacher capacity and instructional clarity unaddressed.

summaries.headline: CoSN Leader Flags New E-rate Threat
summaries.summary: Keith Krueger, longtime head of the Consortium for School Networking, is sounding an alarm over an emerging risk to the federal E-rate program that has underwritten school internet and connectivity for nearly three decades. His warning comes as district technology leaders already navigate funding uncertainty and shifting federal priorities around broadband subsidies. For CTOs and superintendents who've built infrastructure budgets around E-rate reliability, the signal is clear: contingency planning for connectivity funding can no longer wait on the sidelines.

summaries.headline: Louisiana Task Force Reviews Decades-Old School Funding Formula
summaries.summary: A 15-member task force is reviewing Louisiana's Minimum Foundation Program, the formula that has governed how the state distributes $4 billion annually to local school districts for more than 30 years. The group faces the task of recommending a revised or entirely new formula, with nonpartisan advocacy group Leaders for a Better Louisiana stepping in to help explain the MFP's mechanics to stakeholders outside the process. Any changes to this formula could reshape how equitably and effectively state dollars reach classrooms across Louisiana for years to come.

summaries.headline: Iowa Overhauls School Funding Formula for 2026-27
summaries.summary: Iowa lawmakers have enacted new legislation that will reshape how state dollars flow to school districts starting in the 2026-27 school year. The full text of the bill's mechanics wasn't available in this source, but the shift signals a departure from the state's existing per-pupil funding approach, with winners and losers likely to emerge among districts depending on enrollment trends and local property wealth. District finance officers should watch for detailed guidance from the Iowa Department of Education on how the new formula affects their specific allocations well before budget season begins.

summaries.headline: Colorado Names First Five Teacher of the Year Finalists
summaries.summary: Colorado education officials named five of the eight finalists for the 2027 Colorado Teacher of the Year award, narrowed from 21 semifinalists selected in June out of nearly 300 applications from 76 districts. The finalists span a computer science teacher in Douglas County, a Trinidad middle school language arts teacher, and an Aurora Spanish teacher recognized for building an inclusive classroom, each surprised with a $1,000 check and a $500 award for their school. Three more finalists arrive next week, with the eventual winner receiving $10,000 and a yearlong turn as a statewide teaching ambassador shaping policy conversations.

summaries.headline: Oklahoma Trains Hundreds of Teachers in Reading Science
summaries.summary: Oklahoma lawmakers overhauled the state's literacy law this year after years of poor reading outcomes, and the first wave of implementation is now underway with 449 teachers completing science-of-reading microcredential training across seven partner universities this summer. The law, modeled on Mississippi's 2013 Literacy-Based Promotion Act, pairs a third-grade retention requirement with expanded coaching and mandates that every district employ a reading specialist, and early results show a 93 percent completion rate among teachers spanning 71 counties and 247 districts. Mississippi's own trajectory under similar policy — climbing from 49th to ninth in fourth-grade NAEP reading — gives Oklahoma, where only 23 percent of fourth graders scored proficient in 2024, a concrete benchmark for what sustained investment in teacher training can yield.

summaries.headline: Montana's Reading Scores Slide Despite National Rankings
summaries.summary: Montana's Office of Public Instruction released its latest school report card showing the state outperforming national averages in math and reading, but the topline numbers mask a steady decline in literacy outcomes. Reading proficiency has dropped nearly 6 percentage points since 2017, and chronic absenteeism continues to worsen even as overall scores hold up relative to other states. The gap between Montana's comparative standing and its internal trendlines suggests state leaders are managing a narrowing advantage rather than a stable success story.

summaries.headline: UNR Teacher Prep Programs Earn Top Marks for Reading
summaries.summary: The University of Nevada, Reno's undergraduate and graduate elementary education programs both received A+ grades from the National Council on Teacher Quality for how well they prepare future teachers to deliver reading instruction. The NCTQ evaluated the programs against five components of scientifically based reading instruction—phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, comprehension and vocabulary—and screened for outdated or ineffective practices, with faculty pointing to more than two decades of emphasis on those core components plus required literacy coursework and supervised tutoring practicums. As states continue tightening reading policy around the science of reading, the report offers a rare, concrete benchmark for which teacher prep programs are actually equipping new teachers to meet those mandates.

summaries.headline: Districts Split on LGBTQ+ Policy Pressure
summaries.summary: School districts across the country are responding in starkly different ways to Trump administration pressure over LGBTQ+ policies, with federal officials including Education Secretary Linda McMahon using investigations and funding threats as leverage. Some districts are revising policies on issues like bathroom access, pronoun use, and gender identity guidance after receiving federal warnings, while others are digging in and contesting the investigations outright. The divergence sets up a patchwork of compliance nationwide and signals that district leaders' tolerance for federal risk, not just local politics, is now shaping policy on the ground.

summaries.headline: Superintendent Flags Chronic Absenteeism as Instructional Crisis
summaries.summary: Fergus Falls Superintendent Jeff Drake opened the school year by directly addressing families about rising chronic absenteeism, a trend he says is playing out across Minnesota and nationally. Drake framed the issue not as a compliance matter but an instructional one, arguing that worksheets sent home can't replace group discussions, lab work, real-time teacher feedback, or peer collaboration that happens in the classroom. His public appeal signals a shift among district leaders toward treating attendance as a shared responsibility requiring family partnership rather than punitive enforcement.

When San Francisco Unified School District leaders announced plans to [increase](https://missionlocal.org/2026/08/sfusd-student-literacy-goals/) third grade literacy scores by 20 percent in two years, parents and educators were nonplussed.

More than half of San Francisco’s students are falling behind in meeting state reading goals. The farthest behind? The district’s most disadvantaged, including students who are low-income, experiencing homelessness, or learning English, and the district’s students of color.

A double-digit increase by 2028 felt like a pipe dream.

But preliminary state testing scores shared exclusively with _Mission Local_ show promise for one pilot program.

Students who are enrolled in the nonprofit [Chapter One](https://www.chapterone.org/?__geom=%E2%9C%AA) program, which provides tutoring for 2,700 students in San Francisco’s “priority schools,” are making gains at almost twice the rate of their peers not enrolled, the reading scores show.

Priority schools are those where at least half of the students are low-income or not yet meeting literacy standards. Students in the program, who are in grades kindergarten through four, are given one-on-one time with trained tutors who enter classrooms four to five times a week, tailoring reading lessons to students’ needs.

The targeted work appears to have paid off, at least for early learners. Kindergarten through second grade students who worked with a Chapter One tutor last year increased their literacy proficiency by 8.2 percent from fall 2025 to spring 2026, compared to only a 4.4 percent increase district wide.

Third graders, who take a different literacy test only once a year, had a more modest 2 percent increase, compared to last year.

Early reading scores are determined by results on the [Star literacy test](https://www.sfusd.edu/district-assessments), an assessment given to students three times a year, once in the fall and again in the spring. The computerized test is created by [Renaissance Leaning](https://www.renaissance.com/about-us/), a software company whose products help schools track student progress. The data comes from last year’s test scores.

The Chapter One program is overseen by the San Francisco Education Fund nonprofit and funded by the city’s Department of Children, Youth and Their Families and the San Francisco Unified School District.

The scores showed that the greatest gains in San Francisco were for those students who historically have had the hardest time meeting their reading goals.

Hispanic students (as they are classified by Chapter One) in kindergarten through second grade who were tutored through Chapter One improved their reading scores more than twice as fast as other Hispanic students in the district who were not enrolled in the program last year, according to their Star scores.

Same goes for English language learners: Chapter One students increased literacy scores by 8.4 percent, while the overall literacy scores of English learners in SFUSD actually dipped from 33.5 percent to 33.1 percent.

Ann Levy Walden, the CEO of the San Francisco Education Fund, said the growth is a testament to persistence — and having an extra educator around.

Tutors are in the classroom. They work with teachers to identify which students need the most help. They spend more time with those students than they do with the students who are farther ahead. They keep showing up, day after day, all school year.

Plus, through separate SFUSD initiatives, teachers have more professional development around literacy and have standardized their curriculum, so all teachers are approaching learning the same way.

“We’ve been calling it a three-legged stool,” Walden said, referring to tutoring, curriculum, and professional development. “That is what’s going to lead our students to have this expanded growth.”

She says even with the small 2 percent increase in third grade literacy, the recent data is fueling optimism.

This school year’s cohort of third graders will take the state’s annual [standardized test](https://www.cde.ca.gov/ta/tg/ca/) in the spring. Levy hopes, with more students than ever having been in Chapter One, they will score high and help the district inch closer to its 70 percent goal.

“The district is not moving away from their third grade literacy goal. A less bold district would say, ‘Ugh, this is a stretch,’ but our district is committing to it,” Levy said. “This data is an early indicator that we will have even more growth.”

Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools saw significant student improvement in subjects like math, reading and science from elementary to high school in the 2025-26 school year.

The numbers are in. North Carolina’s annual school accountability reporting showed CMS students across the board grew academically based on end of year test scores.

One notable gain was in literacy, with 76.9% of third-graders reaching proficiency through North Carolina's Read to Achieve program. Between grades 3-8, reading improved 4 points, up to 56.7%, and in English II, students improved 6.8 points to 66%.

Other notable gains include math scores. In grades 3-8, math proficiency improved 3.5 points, to 62.7%; High school Math 1 rose 13 points, up to 42%; High school Math 3 increased 2.8 points to 69.4%.

Fifth to eighth graders improved science scores by 7.6 points, up to 69.3%. Biology scores also improved almost 10 points to 58.4% proficient.

Schools also improved scores from the previous year. Three schools improved enough to leave behind the "low-performing" status. This year, 28 schools were deemed low-performing, versus last year's 31.

Just under 80% of CMS schools earned at least a C grade for performance, a 8 point increase from 2024-25.

More students also graduated this year from the previous. 87.9% of students walked the stage in 2026, which was 3.3 points higher than last year.

“This progress belongs to our students, teachers, school leaders, staff and families,” Superintendent Dr. Crystal Hill said. “These results show what is possible when we remain focused on strong instruction, high expectations and providing every student with the support they need to succeed. We are proud of the progress our students are making, and we remain committed to building on this momentum.”

Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools is celebrating another year of academic progress, with nearly 79% of schools earning an A, B or C performance grade.

District leaders say the results mark another historic year for CMS, but they acknowledge there is still work to do — particularly when it comes to achievement gaps.

The end-of-year state accountability results show CMS outperformed North Carolina in overall grade-level proficiency and college and career readiness. The district also saw significant increases in reading, math and Math 1.

### Literacy among notable areas of improvement

One of the district’s biggest achievements came in literacy.

Nearly 77% of CMS third graders — 76.9% — demonstrated proficiency.

At Ashley Park Pre-K in West Charlotte, Principal Joline Adams says the school has made significant progress over the past two years.

“In the last two years, we have moved two letter grades. We were an F to a D, and now, we moved from a D to a C.”

Adams credits the improvement to creating strong systems, consistency and being willing to adjust when something isn’t working.

“Creating strong systems, structures and consistency and never giving up and being able to reflect on what is not working and what do we need to do differently.”

### District still faces challenges

While nearly 79% of CMS schools earned an A, B or C, about 21% received a D or F.

Two CMS schools currently meet the state’s definition of an F.

Deputy Superintendent Dr. Melissa Balknight says the district believes it knows how to help those schools improve.

“We do have two schools that have the state definition of an F. However, we believe that we have a pretty good track record now that we know how to support our schools to be successful, and we fully anticipate that we’ll remove them from the list at the end of this year.”

School board chair Stephanie Sneed says the district cannot lose focus on closing education gaps.

“We got to keep pressing. We definitely have to close education gaps, without question.”

CMS also says it is not satisfied with the current achievement gaps across the district.

“We are not satisfied with where we stand right now in terms of achievement gaps,” CMS’ Beth Thompson said.

### Superintendent speaks in Raleigh

Superintendent Dr. Crystal Hill was not at the CMS meeting.

She was in Raleigh meeting with the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction, where she discussed the steps CMS took to achieve the latest results.

District leaders say the progress is encouraging, but the focus now shifts to sustaining that momentum and improving outcomes for students and schools that continue to struggle.

[Share on Facebook](https://www.heraldguide.com/featured/school-playgroups-promote-early-literacy-kindergarten-readiness/# "Share on Facebook")[Tweet This Post](https://www.heraldguide.com/featured/school-playgroups-promote-early-literacy-kindergarten-readiness/# "Tweet This Post")[Pin This Post](https://www.heraldguide.com/featured/school-playgroups-promote-early-literacy-kindergarten-readiness/# "Pin This Post")[Share on Google+](https://www.heraldguide.com/featured/school-playgroups-promote-early-literacy-kindergarten-readiness/# "Share on Google+")[Send this article to a friend](mailto:?subject=School%20playgroups%20promote%20early%20literacy%2C%20kindergarten%20readiness%C2%A0&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.heraldguide.com%2Ffeatured%2Fschool-playgroups-promote-early-literacy-kindergarten-readiness%2F "Send this article to a friend")

St. Charles Parish Public Schools is continuing its playgroup program this school year, giving families with young children a chance to build early literacy and other skills before they start Pre-K or kindergarten.

The playgroups, which serve children 4 years old and younger, will be offered at Mimosa Park, New Sarpy, Allemands, Norco, Luling and St. Rose elementary schools through May.

Playgroups begin at 10 a.m. every other week at each school. Sessions are held Mondays at Mimosa Park and New Sarpy elementary schools, Wednesdays at Allemands and Norco elementary schools, and Thursdays at Luling and St. Rose elementary schools. Families may attend playgroups at any location, regardless of where they live in the parish.

The program is free and is supported through a combination of local district money and federal funds.

Patricia Smith, director of federal programs for the district, said the playgroups are part of the district’s effort to improve kindergarten readiness and increase family engagement.

“Our playgroups help families and children get a feel for what school looks like and sounds like,” Smith said. “And now that we have universal Pre-K, we’re hoping some of our 4-year-olds that come to the playgroup will be encouraged to go ahead and start Pre-K.”

Smith said one of the program’s biggest goals is helping parents understand that early literacy can be incorporated into everyday life.

“First, we want to make sure we’re sending books home,” she said. “But we’re also teaching parents that literacy is a natural everyday occurrence. Language is developed when you’re looking at your child and your child is looking at you, and they see you pronouncing the words.”

The playgroups begin with center time, when children can play and interact with one another while parents participate alongside them. The sessions then include music and movement, oral language activities, phonemic awareness exercises, reading and a hands-on activity connected to the lesson.

Local librarians have participated in playgroups in previous years, and Smith said the district also plans to occasionally bring in additional specialists, including speech therapists.

Smith said parents often notice their children gaining new skills after attending the playgroups.

“Parents will tell us, you know, my child is starting to participate and play with other kids,” Smith said. “They’re starting to talk more.”

The playgroups are led by educators and liaisons at the district’s Family Learning Centers, which are located at Mimosa Park, New Sarpy, Allemands, Norco, Luling and St. Rose elementary schools. Those centers are tasked with increasing family engagement and serving as resources for parents and families.

The Learning Centers also partner with United Way to offer community playgroups on Tuesdays through its Learn With Us Bus, a mobile learning center that brings playgroup activities into neighborhoods throughout the parish.

# Delaware Valley High School seniors learn financial literacy

### Young Life. Students also awarded $1250 each in scholarship funds through Charles Petesheim’s fund at The Community Foundation of Orange, Sullivan and Rockland.

[Milford](https://www.pikecountycourier.com/tag/-/meta/milford) /


\| 03 Sep 2026 \| 10:04


![Delaware Valley High School seniors learn financial literacy](https://www.pikecountycourier.com/binrepository/576x432/0c0/0d0/none/1107792/SPEP/img-0086_4-11067141_20260903100442.jpg)

Charles Petersheim, owner of Sullivan County-based builder Catskill Farms, recently sponsored and taught his second annual financial literacy class to seniors at Delaware Valley High School. This year’s class consisted of eight students, each of whom was awarded a $1,250 scholarship via his fund at The Community Foundation of Orange, Sullivan and Rockland after attending a two-hour class.

“Financial awareness and developing good habits are key ingredients to a good life,” Petersheim said. “It’s helpful to start building those habits early. This seminar gives the kids some helpful tips to augment whatever they are learning at home and school.”

Petersheim praised the students for their accomplishments and emphasized the importance of combining educational opportunities with real-world financial knowledge.

“Programs like this help students take their next step with confidence,” said Rick Little, executive director of Greater Pike Community Foundation. “We congratulate this year’s recipients and thank Chuck Petersheim, who provided both a scholarship and skills they’ll draw on for years.”

**This year’s Tri-State Financial Literacy scholarship recipients are:**

Shaun Cannalley, Reagan Decker, Chris Devaney, Ashantia Dicette, Joclyn Dzyak, Mike Iuzzolino, Riley Smith and Savannah Van Orden.

Petersheim also advises the Petersheim Fund at Greater Pike Community Foundation. Online donations to that fund or any other fund administered by Greater Pike can be made at [www.greaterpike.org/funds](http://www.greaterpike.org/funds).

# Bittersweet celebration, Rotary honors Dolly Parton’s life and literacy legacy

BY JO NIEUWSMA

[![Mayor Amy Howard reads a proclamation in honor of Dolly Parton and her Imagination Library in front of the Port Townsend Library Aug. 26. The event was a Rotary Club celebration marking the five-year anniversary of the Imagination Library program in Jefferson County. Photo courtesy of Jo Nieuwsma](https://ptleader.com/wp-content/uploads/images/2026-09-02/31p1-2048x1082.jpg)](https://ptleader.com/wp-content/uploads/images/2026-09-02/31p1-scaled.jpg)

Mayor Amy Howard reads a proclamation in honor of Dolly Parton and her Imagination Library in front of the Port Townsend Library Aug. 26. The event was a Rotary Club celebration marking the five-year anniversary of the Imagination Library program in Jefferson County. Photo courtesy of Jo Nieuwsma

In a sadly ironic twist, worthy of a country western ballad, The Port Townsend Rotary Club had planned a celebration Aug. 26 of its support for the last five years of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in Jefferson County when it was announced we had lost her. The event became a celebration of Dolly’s life.

Port Townsend Mayor Amy Howard read a proclamation in honor of Dolly and her wonderful program. Melody Sky Weaver our head librarian spoke about the process for bringing the program to Jefferson County and how she was able to meet Dolly when she was just 3. Fellow Rotarians, City Council member David Faber and Jefferson Healthcare Chief Operating Officer Jake Davidson each spoke about how much the program has meant to their children.

The Port Townsend Rotary Club, a philanthropic club, run by volunteers and funded by membership dues, started in 1929 so it’s getting close to celebrating 100 years.

In only the last few years, Port Townsend Rotary club has supported many local organizations with well over $200,000 in scholarships for both college as well as occupational students, small and large grants to local and international operations, inbound and outbound exchange students to many countries all over the world, and more.

Port Townsend Rotary also does many volunteer projects around the area, maintaining several small parks, helping local food bank grower gardens, international projects for clean water, eradication of polio in the world, betterment of people’s lives and in 2021, bringing Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library to Jefferson County’s children.

Five years ago we took on local support to help pay for free books to be mailed every month to local kids from birth to age five. Since then, the DPIL program in Jefferson County has grown to cover about 450 children a month and in the five years we have supported it, there have been almost 1,000 kids in the program, sending over 26,000 books so far.

The Imagination Library has been in existence for over 30 years and has provided more than 300 million books to children in five countries. New books are chosen each year, 12 books for each tier (based on age) and multiple kids get different books

The Raker’s Car Club was represented at the event to honor Mr. David Harrah who was also lost to us just recently. He was a founding sponsor who generously helped us get the Imagination Library program started here in Jefferson County.

The club offered great appreciation to the initial sponsors of the program: David Harrah, Lynn Marlow, Carol Wise- Coldwell Banker Best Homes, Cunnington Dental, Lynette Jennings, Nieuwsma Trust and Port Townsend Shipwrights Coop.

Rotary International is ranked four stars by Charity Navigator for the best of charities with almost all proceeds being returned to the community.

Jo Nieuwsma is the Rotary public image chair and Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library minion.

While Dolly Parton may not have been from Kentucky, her impact on the literacy and education of children in the commonwealth is undeniable.

Currently 850 children in Marshall County are enrolled in the Imagination Library program.

The Marshall County branch of the program is facilitated by the Marshall County Public Library as one of many ways the library aims to facilitate early childhood literacy. In recent years, the Kentucky state legislature opted to provide 50% of the necessary funding to each county for the program.

Marshall County Public Library Director Tammy Blackwell shared that the Joe Tom Haltom Foundation provides an additional approximately 45% of the county’s funds.

Blackwell emphasized the importance of the program, stating that the ability for children to access quality, age appropriate books has been repeatedly linked to success later in life.

“Studies show the most important indicator of future academic success is having access to age-appropriate books when they’re young,” Blackwell said. “More than education level of the parents, or parents’ career, or income. Those things that we really think play into it a lot are not as important as having access to age appropriate books.”

While providing that access is the primary goal of the Imagination Library program, it is also a general library mission. Blackwell noted that the history of the modern library model traces back to Andrew Carnegie and his desire to provide better access than he had received.

“In the United States, really, a lot of our core, who we are as libraries, comes from Andrew Carnegie, who went from having nothing to being the richest man in the world due to books, due to studying, and putting into himself,” Blackwell said. “He said that everybody should have that opportunity, and so he funded libraries all across the nation, and I really think that’s made a huge impact in America, how we view libraries.”

Providing that access to books, particularly through the Imagination Library program, is a mission of personal importance to Blackwell, as well as a professional one. Blackwell’s own mother is originally from Appalachia, and her father — Blackwell’s grandfather — was unable to read or write.

“My mom is also from Appalachia,” said Blackwell. “She’s from the Kentucky part, not the Tennessee part, but her father also could not read or write. I think he made it to maybe the second grade. Here in our modern times, it’s hard to wrap our brains around that, that there was a time, and not that long ago, where kids weren’t necessarily getting the education they needed, and didn’t have literacy skills. I think it’s beautiful that \[Parton\] saw this and saw how it impacted his life, and said, ‘I don’t want that to happen to anyone else.’ ”

The library also participates in a nationwide program called “1,000 Books Before Kindergarten,” which, as the title suggests, encourages children to have read — or read to them — 1,000 books before they begin kindergarten.

“We have prizes and different goals along the way, and encourage that, but it’s that a child gets a thousand books read to them before they start kindergarten,” Blackwell said. “Because again, the impact that has on their ability to succeed, not only in kindergarten, but beyond kindergarten, is...just really important. So, we encourage parents to read 1,000 books before that kid hits that age. With ‘1,000 Books Before Kindergarten,’ it doesn’t matter if you’re reading the same book 10 times, that’s 10 books on that path, because even that repeated exposure, it’s giving them a better understanding of the story. It’s giving them what those words mean. It’s a really great program.”

Those interested in registering for the Imagination Library can do so online, but assistance is available at the Marshall County Public Library if needed. Blackwell noted that it can take “a couple of months” for an Imagination Library registration to process, but to reach out to the library if three months passes before the first book is received.

Those interested in donating to the Marshall County branch of the Imagination Library can do so by writing a check to the Marshall County Imagination Library or by donating online at the Imagination Library website. Online donations can still be specified to particular areas.
